name: Automatisch
tagline: Trigger-and-action flows on your own box, with a connector list you can count and no credit meter.

local.note: Triggers are checked every fifteen minutes and only while this computer is awake, and the webhook address Automatisch hands a third-party service begins with http://localhost:8171, which that service cannot reach.

quote.text: Please be careful with the ENCRYPTION_KEY and WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY environment variables. They are used to encrypt your credentials from third-party services and verify webhook requests. If you change them, your existing connections and flows will not continue to work.

citations.claim: Upstream's Docker install runs two services from the same image with the same environment, main and worker, differing only by WORKER=true.
The Available apps page for the release this install pins lists 82 integrations, against the thousands Make advertises.
The community edition is AGPL-3.0, and every file whose name contains .ee. is covered instead by a separate commercial Enterprise licence.
Without a valid enterprise licence, a flow's execution interval is forced back to fifteen minutes and every polling trigger runs on a fifteen-minute cron.
The endpoint that creates the first admin account refuses with 403 once installation is complete or any user exists, which is what closes the door behind the first signup.

whatYouSignUpFor: You become the developer at every service you connect. The release pinned here documents 82 integrations, and 39 of them present a redirect URL you have to paste into a developer console at that company and copy a client id and secret back. Make's price is partly a set of app registrations somebody else already holds, and moving the software does not move those.

The catalogue is the gap, and the shape of a flow is the other one. A flow is one trigger and a line of actions, with a filter step that can stop the run. There are no routers, no iterators and no aggregators, so a Make scenario that forks down two paths does not have an equivalent here; you build two flows.

Fifteen minutes is the floor. Without an enterprise licence every polling trigger is scheduled on a fifteen-minute cron, and a flow saved with a shorter interval is put back to fifteen. Webhook triggers fire immediately, which is the reason the cloud path wants a real hostname and the local path honestly gives you half the tool.

The core is AGPL-3.0, and every file with .ee. in its name is under a separate commercial licence instead. That split is where the public REST API, SAML, roles and permissions, templates and the sub-fifteen-minute scheduler live. What you install is uncapped on flows, runs and connections and stops short of that list.

Check the cadence before you commit. v0.15.0 was tagged in August 2025 and the last commit to the repository was in February 2026, so a connector that breaks when a third party changes an endpoint may stay broken until someone sends a patch. This is the risk you are taking on in exchange for the bill, and it is a real one.
